name: Stonehenge
dateLabel: c. 3000–2500 BCE · earthwork and main stone circle
significance: A ceremonial landscape links large-scale communal building with burial and the seasonal movement of the sun.
lookFor: Follow the axis of the stone circle toward the Heel Stone and notice the lintels joining the upright sarsens.
constructionNote: Earthworks began around 3000 BCE; the main stone circle was raised around 2500 BCE, with rearrangements continuing later.

name: Diocletian’s Palace
style: Late Roman imperial and fortified architecture
civilization: Roman Empire · Diocletian and the Tetrarchy
significance: An imperial residence became the living fabric of a medieval city; Roman rooms and streets still shape central Split.
lookFor: Compare the columned Peristyle, palace gates and vaulted substructures with the houses inserted into the Roman plan.
constructionNote: The late third- to early fourth-century complex was ready for Diocletian’s retirement in 305; medieval and later buildings occupy its walls and courtyards.

name: Aachen Cathedral · Palatine Chapel
style: Carolingian / pre-Romanesque, with later Gothic additions
significance: Charlemagne’s palace chapel joined Roman and Byzantine building traditions to a new imperial centre north of the Alps.
lookFor: Identify the domed octagon and upper gallery, then compare their massing with the tall glazed Gothic choir.
constructionNote: Dates refer to the early medieval octagonal core. The Gothic choir was completed in 1414; the present dome mosaic dates to 1880–1881.

name: Urnes Stave Church
style: Timber stave architecture with Romanesque forms and Viking carving
civilization: Medieval Kingdom of Norway · Christianization and Nordic traditions
significance: A wooden basilica preserves the meeting of Scandinavian craftsmanship and medieval Christian church design.
lookFor: Find the interlaced animals on the reused north portal, then compare them with the carved column capitals inside.
constructionNote: The present church is dated around 1130 by its operator; carved elements around 1070 were reused from an earlier church, and later alterations survive.

name: Westminster Abbey
style: English Gothic, with later Perpendicular Gothic and west towers
civilization: Medieval Kingdom of England · Plantagenet monarchy
significance: Royal patronage turned an older abbey into a Gothic setting for coronations, royal tombs and national memory.
lookFor: Look up at pointed arches and rib vaults, and compare the medieval eastern church with Henry VII’s later fan-vaulted chapel.
constructionNote: The dates cover the apse, chapels, transepts and quire rebuilt under Henry III; the nave, Henry VII’s chapel and west towers belong to later campaigns.
coordinateSource: De Montfort University / Shakespearean London Theatres: https://shalt.dmu.ac.uk/locations/westminster-abbey-poets-corner.html

name: Cologne Cathedral
civilization: Medieval Rhineland / Holy Roman Empire; completed in the German Empire
significance: A medieval cathedral project was completed six centuries later with sustained fidelity to its Gothic design.
lookFor: Compare the medieval choir and stained glass with the huge west façade and spires completed in the nineteenth century.
constructionNote: Construction began in 1248, paused for centuries and was completed in 1880; the range describes distinct campaigns rather than continuous work.

name: Malbork Castle
style: Brick Gothic fortified monastery and palace
civilization: Teutonic Order’s state in Prussia; later a Polish royal residence
significance: A military religious order built a fortified administrative capital that later passed to the Polish Crown.
lookFor: Trace the red-brick defensive rings and distinguish the High Castle, Middle Castle and Grand Masters’ Palace.
constructionNote: The complex grew in stages from the late thirteenth to mid-fifteenth century; extensive nineteenth-century restoration and reconstruction after 1945 shaped today’s fabric.
sourceName: Malbork Castle Museum · History of the Castle

name: St Vitus Cathedral
dateLabel: 1344–1929 CE · medieval core and modern completion
style: Gothic with nineteenth- and twentieth-century Neo-Gothic completion
civilization: Kingdom of Bohemia · Luxembourg dynasty and Holy Roman Empire
significance: A royal cathedral expresses Prague’s role as the seat of Charles IV and preserves the burial and coronation traditions of Bohemia.
lookFor: Compare the medieval choir and St Wenceslas Chapel with the later west front and modern stained glass.
constructionNote: The Gothic cathedral began in 1344 on the site of older churches; after long interruptions its completion was celebrated in 1929.
sourceName: Prague Castle Administration · St Vitus Cathedral
coordinateSource: Building coordinates in the cathedral operator’s linked map: https://www.katedralasvatehovita.cz/en/about-the-cathedral/contact/

name: Brussels Town Hall
style: Brabantine Gothic with later classical courtyard wings
civilization: Duchy of Brabant · Burgundian Low Countries and urban government
significance: A monumental civic hall reveals the political confidence of a prosperous medieval trading city.
lookFor: Compare the slender Gothic tower and asymmetrical façade with the surrounding Grand-Place guild houses.
constructionNote: The medieval hall and tower were built in several phases; it partly survived the 1695 bombardment, with later wings and nineteenth-century sculptural restoration.
coordinateSource: Approximate building point beside UNESCO Grand-Place property point: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/857/

name: Voroneț Monastery · St George Church
style: Moldavian Orthodox architecture with Byzantine and late Gothic influences
civilization: Principality of Moldavia · Stephen the Great and Orthodox patronage
significance: Painted exterior walls turn a regional Orthodox church into a public cycle of sacred stories.
lookFor: Find the west-wall Last Judgment, blue background and pointed stone window frames beneath the projecting roof.
constructionNote: The church was built in 1488, with an enclosed porch added in 1547; its Byzantine influences belong to Moldavian artistic traditions.
sourceName: Romania National Heritage Institute / CIMEC · Voroneț
coordinateSource: Approximate church point; National Archaeological Repertory site map: https://ran.cimec.ro/sel.asp?Lang=EN&descript=voronet-oras-gura-humorului-suceava-manastirea-voronet-cod-sit-ran-146600.01

name: St Paul’s Cathedral
civilization: Restoration England and early Great Britain · Anglican church
significance: Christopher Wren’s cathedral gave rebuilt London a monumental dome after the Great Fire of 1666.
lookFor: Compare the classical west portico with the rising dome, paired towers and dramatic approach steps.
constructionNote: Wren rebuilt the cathedral after the medieval building burned in 1666. Worship began in 1697; Parliament declared the new cathedral complete in 1711.

name: Schönbrunn Palace
civilization: Habsburg Monarchy · Maria Theresa and the imperial court
significance: The summer palace organised court ceremony, dynastic display and imperial life along a grand garden axis.
lookFor: Follow the palace’s central axis into the gardens and compare the ordered façades with the mirrored, gilded Rococo rooms.
constructionNote: An earlier palace began in 1696. The dates focus on Maria Theresa’s rebuilding from 1743 and the major furnishing campaign into the mid-1760s.
coordinateSource: Approximate palace point in UNESCO palace-and-gardens property: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/786/maps/

name: Hungarian Parliament Building
style: Gothic Revival with Renaissance and Baroque influences
civilization: Kingdom of Hungary within Austria-Hungary · parliamentary and national identity
significance: A monumental parliament on the Danube projected Hungarian political identity during the Dual Monarchy.
lookFor: Compare the pointed riverside spires with the central dome and symmetrical arrangement of the two assembly wings.
constructionNote: Construction began in 1885. Parliamentary offices and sittings moved in during 1902, and building work was fully completed in 1904.
coordinateSource: Approximate building point at Kossuth Lajos tér, verified against official Parliament visitor location: https://latogatokozpont.parlament.hu/en/home

name: Stockholm City Hall
style: National Romantic, with Renaissance and Swedish Baroque references
civilization: Modern Sweden · municipal government and national heritage
significance: Ragnar Östberg combined historic Swedish building traditions with Venetian references for a modern city’s civic centre.
lookFor: Compare the red brick, waterfront colonnade and Three Crowns tower with the palace-like courtyards.
constructionNote: The City Hall was built from 1911 to 1923. Its historic-looking forms were deliberately selected for a twentieth-century civic building.
sourceName: City of Stockholm · City Hall history
coordinateSource: Approximate building point at the official address Hantverkargatan 1: https://stadshuset.stockholm/en/plan-your-visit/getting-here/

name: Rietveld Schröder House
civilization: Interwar Netherlands · De Stijl artistic movement
significance: Gerrit Rietveld and client Truus Schröder transformed a family house into an experiment in open space, movable partitions and abstract form.
lookFor: Notice primary-colour accents, independent horizontal and vertical planes, and the flexible upper-floor arrangement.
constructionNote: Built in 1924 and inhabited for six decades; conservation in the 1970s and 1980s restored the design and interiors toward their 1920s condition.

name: Bauhaus Building
civilization: Weimar Republic · Bauhaus school of art, design and architecture
significance: Walter Gropius gave an experimental design school a building whose connected wings make their different functions visible.
lookFor: Study the workshop’s glass curtain wall, the bridge between wings and the contrast between glazed and solid surfaces.
constructionNote: The school building dates to 1925–1926; wartime damage and later restorations are part of the surviving building’s history.
